To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the assays recently introduced to characterize transdermals are not completely suitable to characterize medicated plasters.

the adhesive performances of medicated plastrons can be assessed by using EMA draft and USP specific tests and that the in vitro skin permeations can be performed by using the EMA draft and the USP specific tests, provided that a novel calculation of the efficiency of MP is used.

the adhesive performances of MP are comparable to that of TP, but a modification of the test procedure for shear adhesion is required, the mass balance of the in vitro skin permeability test should be revised, and finally the in vitro skin penetration studies could be used to evaluate the efficacy of MP in releasing drug through the skin.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods to characterize MP and to evaluate the in vitro efficiency in releasing the drug through the skin, which are useful for the pharmaceutical industry.
the characterization of MP according to new requirements of EMA and USP and the results are promising for the application of the proposed methods in the pharmaceutical industry.
the development and validation of new analytical methods for the characterization of medicaments for external use.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the new EMA and USP guidelines are not suitable for the characterization of MP.
, even if the assays recently proposed by EMA and USP to characterize TP are not completely suitable for MP, some of them are suitable and some others need to be improved or replaced.
EMA draft and USP requirements for the characterization of MP are not fully suitable and that some modifications are necessary.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

EMA and USP guidelines for transdermal patches could be applied to MP, but the adhesive properties of MP need to be evaluated by specific methods and a more suitable range of acceptance for the in vitro permeation studies needs to be established.

the assays introduced by EMA and USP are suitable for MP but the acceptance range of the mass balance for in vitro penetration studies is too narrow and the shear adhesion test should be modified for MP containing an adhesive hydrogel.
the new EMA and USP requirements for the characterization of TP can be applied to MP but with a few adjustments.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the assays introduced by EMA and USP to characterize TP can be used to characterize MP, provided some modifications.
the EMA and USP assays are not suitable for MP, and that the in vitro skin permeability of MP should be evaluated in terms of in vitro efficiency.
the EMA draft guideline and the USP specific tests for transdermals patches can be used to characterize medicated plasters.
